title: Where things are
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: -e and -eseo split one English word by what the sentence is DOING. -e marks where something is, or where it is going. -eseo marks where an action takes place. hakgyo-e isseoyo, 'I am at school'; hakgyo-eseo gongbuhaeyo, 'I study at school'. English uses 'at' for both, so nothing in your own language warns you which one is needed — look at the verb.
A place you are going to takes -e, never -eseo: hakgyo-e gayo. Going is not an action that happens AT the school; the school is the point you end up at, and -e is the marker for a point.

isseoyo does the work English splits between 'there is' and 'is at'. A thing at a place simply exists at that place, so the verb you learned for having and existing is the same one you use for location — and eopseoyo says the same thing about something absent.

Position words are NOUNS. wi is 'the top', yeop is 'the side', and they follow the thing they belong to and then take their own marker: chaeksang wi-e, 'desk top-at'. English puts a preposition in front of the noun; Korean puts a noun behind it and marks the pair.
eodi ('where') behaves like any other place: it takes -e and it sits where a place sits. The question is still made by the voice alone — eodi-e isseoyo? — and nothing about the word order changes.
What exists takes -i or -ga, not the object marker. chaek-i chaeksang wi-e isseoyo. Nothing is being acted on in a sentence about location, so there is no object for -eul or -reul to mark.

'House', and 'home' — Korean does not separate the building from the idea of home, so jip-e gayo is 'I am going home'.
The same marker again, now marking where something IS or where it is going: jip-e isseoyo, hakgyo-e gayo. One ending, one job — putting something at a point — whether the point is an hour or a house.
'There is', from M3 — and the verb of being somewhere. Korean has no separate verb for location: a thing at a place simply exists at that place, so one word does both jobs.

sentences.trap: The verb here is the one you learned for 'there is' and 'I have'. English changes verb entirely for location — 'I am at home' — and Korean does not: being somewhere is existing at that point.

sentences.cue: The book is on the desk.

words.note: 'Book', from M1. Here it is the thing that exists, so it takes -i.
'Desk' — chaek ('book') plus sang ('table'). Korean builds a great many nouns by stacking two like this, and knowing one half often gives you the meaning.
'The top of something' — a NOUN, not a preposition: it follows the thing it is on and takes its own marker, chaeksang wi-e, 'desk top-at'. English puts 'on' in front; Korean puts a noun behind.
The same marker again, now marking where something IS or where it is going: jip-e isseoyo, hakgyo-e gayo. One ending, one job — putting something at a point — whether the point is an hour or a house.
'There is', from M3 — and the verb of being somewhere. Korean has no separate verb for location: a thing at a place simply exists at that place, so one word does both jobs.

sentences.trap: There is no word here meaning 'on'. wi is a noun — 'the top' — and it follows the desk and takes its own marker, so the whole thing reads as 'desk top-at'. An English speaker will look for a preposition and find a noun.
sentences.sound: CHAE-gi CHAEK-sang WI-e i-SSUH-yo. chaek softens to chae-gi in front of -i, and chaeksang keeps its k hard because sang begins with a consonant. wi is a single beat, close to English 'we'.
